questions.prompt: What happens to a struct's memberwise initializer when you add a custom initializer in an extension?

options.text: The automatic memberwise initializer is permanently deleted.
options.explanation: Declaring initializers inside the struct body deletes it, but extensions preserve it.

options.text: The compiler emits a conflicting initializer error.
options.explanation: Extensions can add initializers without conflicting with the memberwise initializer.

options.text: The struct keeps both initializers available for use.
options.explanation: Right. Adding an initializer in an extension preserves the memberwise initializer.

options.text: The custom initializer is downgraded to convenience.
options.explanation: Structs do not have convenience initializers; all struct initializers are value initializers.

questions.prompt: What kind of initializers can an extension add to a class?

options.text: Designated initializers only.
options.explanation: Designated initializers must be declared in the primary class definition.

options.text: Required initializers only.
options.explanation: Required designated initializers belong in the main class body.

options.text: Both designated and convenience initializers.
options.explanation: Extensions on classes are restricted to convenience initializers.

options.text: Convenience initializers only.
options.explanation: Right. Class extensions can only define convenience initializers.

questions.prompt: What capability do protocol extensions provide in Swift?

options.text: They allow protocols to store weak delegate properties.
options.explanation: Protocols cannot store properties even through extensions.

options.text: They convert all conforming types into reference classes.
options.explanation: Value types retain their value semantics when conforming.

options.text: They eliminate the need for protocol witness tables.
options.explanation: Witness tables are still used for protocol dispatch.

options.text: They supply default implementations of protocol requirements.
options.explanation: Right. Protocol extensions provide default method and property logic to conforming types.

options.text: Yes, extensions can define and use new nested types.
options.explanation: Right. Extensions can introduce new nested enums, structs, or classes.

options.text: No, nested types must reside in the main definition.
options.explanation: Extensions fully support declaring new nested types.

options.text: Only if the parent type is a final class.
options.explanation: Nested types can be added to structs, enums, and non-final classes.

options.text: Only within Swift package manager manifest files.

questions.prompt: How does method dispatch differ for a method declared in a protocol versus one declared ONLY in a protocol extension?

options.text: Both use dynamic message sending via Objective-C.
options.explanation: Pure Swift protocol dispatch uses witness tables or direct calls.

options.text: Protocol requirements dispatch dynamically; extension-only methods dispatch statically.
options.explanation: Right. Methods in the protocol blueprint use dynamic witness dispatch; extension-only methods use static direct dispatch.

options.text: Protocol requirements dispatch statically; extension-only methods dispatch dynamically.
options.explanation: The reverse is true: blueprint methods use dynamic witness dispatch.

options.text: Both methods always use direct static inline dispatch.
options.explanation: Blueprint methods allow dynamic customization across conforming types.

questions.prompt: Why are extensions commonly used in iOS development to organize code?

options.text: They force the compiler to allocate code into separate threads.
options.explanation: Extensions do not manage concurrency or thread dispatch.

options.text: They group protocol conformances and related methods into modular blocks.
options.explanation: Right. Separating protocol implementations into extensions keeps files clean and organized.

options.text: They eliminate the need for unit testing.
options.explanation: Code inside extensions must be tested just like any other code.

questions.prompt: Explain what Swift extensions can add to existing types and what capabilities they cannot add.

rubric.criterion: Lists capabilities extensions can add: computed properties, methods, initializers, subscripts, protocol conformances
Lists restrictions extensions cannot do: cannot add stored properties, property observers to existing properties, or override existing methods

questions.modelAnswer: Extensions can add computed properties, instance and type methods, new initializers, subscripts, nested types, and protocol conformances to existing types. However, extensions cannot add stored properties, cannot attach property observers to existing stored properties, and cannot override existing methods.

questions.prompt: How does defining a custom initializer in an extension preserve a struct's automatic memberwise initializer?

rubric.criterion: Explains that declaring an initializer in the main struct definition suppresses the compiler-generated memberwise initializer
Explains that declaring the custom initializer in an extension keeps both the memberwise initializer and the custom initializer active

questions.modelAnswer: If you define a custom initializer inside a struct primary body, Swift removes the automatic memberwise initializer. However, if you declare your custom initializer in an extension, Swift preserves the automatic memberwise initializer, making both initializers available to callers.

questions.prompt: What is retroactive modeling in Swift, and how do extensions enable it?

rubric.criterion: Explains that retroactive modeling is making existing types conform to protocols without modifying their original source code
Explains that extensions allow external types (like Standard Library or third-party types) to adopt custom protocols

questions.modelAnswer: Retroactive modeling is the practice of extending an existing type to conform to a protocol without modifying its original source code. Using an extension, you can make types from the Swift Standard Library, Apple frameworks, or third-party packages adopt your own custom protocols cleanly.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference in method dispatch between a method declared in a protocol definition versus a method declared only in a protocol extension.

rubric.criterion: Explains that methods declared in the protocol definition dispatch dynamically through protocol witness tables, allowing conforming types to customize them
Explains that methods declared only in protocol extensions dispatch statically (direct dispatch), preventing dynamic customization

questions.modelAnswer: When a method is declared in the protocol definition and implemented in an extension, it uses dynamic dispatch via protocol witness tables. Conforming types can override it. If a method is declared only in an extension, it uses static direct dispatch and cannot be overridden dynamically.

questions.prompt: Why are class extensions restricted to convenience initializers rather than designated initializers?

rubric.criterion: Explains that designated initializers make sure all stored properties introduced by the class are initialized
Explains that convenience initializers delegate across to designated initializers, preventing broken initialization hierarchies across files

questions.modelAnswer: Class extensions can only add convenience initializers because designated initializers are responsible for initializing all stored properties and delegating up to superclasses. Allowing designated initializers in extensions across different files could compromise compiler initialization guarantees. Convenience initializers safely delegate across to existing designated initializers.
